newsitem.title: JAPAN: Weak yen curbs "reverse" import of Japanese cars.
newsitem.headline: Weak yen curbs "reverse" import of Japanese cars.

text.p: For the first time since Japanese auto giants began making cars overseas and shipping them to their home market, annual sales of these "re-imported" vehicles may drop this year because of the weaker yen.

Industry statistics issued Thursday showed that in the first 10 months of the year, domestic sales of Japanese brand cars manufactured overseas fell 13 percent, making it likely that the full-year figures may also register a drop.

After the yen surged from the mid-1980s, Japanese carmakers shifted production to cheaper manufacturing centres overseas, with Honda becoming the first Japanese automaker to "re-import" foreign-built cars in 1988.

Since then, Japanese sales of these "reverse imports" have grown steadily, playing an important role in reducing the vast trade surplus that has long been a source of friction with Japan's biggest trading partner -- the United States.

A Japanese car importers' group said sales of vehicles produced by overseas units of Japanese car makers totalled 76,423 in the January-October period, down 13.1 percent from the same 1995 period as the weaker yen pushed up the cost of re-importing the cars to the home market.

Meanwhile, overall sales of Japanese brand cars in Japan, including those manufactured here, are generally solid, with strong demand for recreational and new sedan models produced by big-name makers such as Toyota and Honda.
Sales of imported Japanese brand cars are likely to total about 92,000 to 93,000 in 1996, down from 106,827 a year earlier, the Japan Automobile Importers Association said.

The car statistics came a day after figures showed that the nation's trade surplus for the first 20 days of October surged from a year earlier, opening up the real possibility of a rise for the month as a whole, due to the weaker yen.
Japan's overall sales of imported vehicles saw a healthy 11.6 percent rise in October to 33,550 units, helped by strong demand for new compact models, the industry group said.

But Ken Kano, the group's planning manager, said sales of imported cars were unlikely to meet the group's target of 450,000 units for this calendar year in the face of declining sales of Japan-brand cars produced abroad.

Sales of Toyota's Sceptre Wagon and Honda's Accord Wagon are relatively slow this year because the cars are expected to be remodelled next year. Kano said the weaker yen was having a big impact on Japanese makers that import cars from their overseas units.
Toyota Motor's Toyota Motor Manufacturing unit in Georgetown, Ky., stopped making the Sceptre station wagon in June because of poor demand in the United States.
Industry sources said Toyota would start producing the Sceptre Wagon in Japan early next year.
Honda is expected to move output of its popular Accord Wagon to Japan from the United States next fall because of the shrinking station wagon market in the United States.

"Even if we face losses due to Toyota and Honda's station wagons next year, we expect growth in 1997 full-year sales because foreign cars excluding Japanese-made are rising firmly with strong demand for compact cars," Kano said.
